Chapter 8: Decision Journals—Creating a Feedback Loop for Growth
Getting better at making decisions isn’t something that just happens on its own. It takes a little work, some honest reflection, and a willingness to learn from what goes right—and, let’s be real, what doesn’t.
One of the best ways to build this kind of feedback loop is by using a decision journal. Think of it as a travel log for your mind. Before you make a big choice, you jot down what you’re thinking, the information you have in front of you, how confident you are, and even what emotions are swirling around. Then, once you know how things turned out, you come back to that entry and see where you nailed it, where you missed the mark, and what you can take with you for next time.
So, why bother with a decision journal? Here are a few reasons that might surprise you.
First, it helps you separate your process from the outcome. By capturing your thoughts before you know what’s going to happen, you get a much clearer picture of your decision-making skills—without letting the end result cloud your memory.
Second, you’ll start to notice patterns over time. Maybe you’re always spot on with financial calls, but you tend to second-guess people decisions. These trends can help you focus on what to improve.
Third, writing things down right as they happen makes it a lot harder to fall into hindsight bias. You can’t quietly rewrite history if all your reasoning is right there in black and white.
And finally, knowing you’ll go back and review your choices later? That encourages a little more care and honesty when you’re making them.
Let’s put this into a real-world example. Imagine you’re a manager who has to pick someone for a new role. You write down why you’re leaning toward a certain candidate, how confident you feel, and any nagging doubts. Fast-forward a few months: you can look back and see how your expectations matched up with reality—and use that insight to improve your hiring process next time.
The best part? Decision journals don’t have to be fancy. Even a couple of sentences for each entry can make a huge difference, as long as you’re consistent and honest with yourself.
So, if you want to get better at making choices, why not give a decision journal a try? It’s a simple habit, but it can change the way you grow—one decision at a time.
